newsitem.title: FRANCE: LVMH signals softer stance toward British groups.
newsitem.headline: LVMH signals softer stance toward British groups.

text.p: French luxury group LVMH signalled on Monday that it might accept as little as 25 percent of the drinks company it wants to create with Guinness and Grand Metropolitan.
The French group's conciliatory stance, expressed in a newspaper controlled by LVMH chairman Bernard Arnault, was interpreted by analysts as being part of the preliminaries to negotiations.
Share analysts said that despite harsh exchanges on Friday, when Guinness and GrandMet slammed Arnault's proposal, it remained in everyone's interest to reach a settlement.
"I'm almost convinced that negotiations have started," one analyst said.
Another French newspaper, Les Echos, said Arnault did insist however on the drinks group being listed independently from the rest of the group which would be created by the Guinness-GrandMet merger.
Arnault initially demanded 35 percent in the 70 billion franc group he has dubbed Drinksco, a stake characterised as unreasonable by the British groups.

LVMH recently said the stake was negotiable, and analysts speculated Arnault would hold out for 30 percent of the group whose portfolio would include the Hennessy, Moet & Chandon, J&B, Smirnoff, Gilbey's, Tanquery, Johnnie Walker and Gordon brands.
Analysts said Arnault looked weakened after the British groups' detailed rebuttal of his claims.

Although it would cost them dearly, they added that they would consider restructuring their merger proposal to require simple majority approval by the shareholders of both companies to get around him.

Currently at least 75 percent of GrandMet shareholders must approve the deal. Arnault has been trying to line up a blocking minority, spending around 12 billion francs to buy 11.06 percent of GrandMet and wooing other investors in the group.

It would cost the British companies roughly 65 million sterling, or more than a third of the 175 million sterling in synergies they envisage, to restructure the deal to lower the approval threshold at GrandMet.
"They would have to justify this before shareholders. I think they're probably leaning toward negotiations," said another analyst.
"The sticking points are control of the drinks unit and the management. Arnault could agree not to take more than 20 or 25 percent for several years."

Another issue to be resolved is what to do with the brewing, canned goods and fast-food businesses. Arnault's proposal called for their de-merger but he signalled flexibility after the British groups said his plan would add 1.5 billion pounds in tax costs.
"LVMH maintains that its plan would create more shareholder value," La Tribune said.

"Determined, if needed, to increase pressure on Guinness and GrandMet to achieve the creation of a listed wines and spirits company, the French group has let it be understood that it would accept bringing the stake it seeks to a minimum of 25 percent," it said.
